title: Linear Classifiers: Logistic Regression & SVMs
summary: Turn a linear score into a class: logistic regression reads it as a probability and trains on cross-entropy, while the SVM asks for a margin and trains on the hinge loss. Kernels then bend the boundary.
takeaways: The sigmoid maps the score z = x·w + b to a probability. Code it stably by branching on the sign of z.
Binary cross-entropy is log(1 + e^z) − y·z, and its gradient (1/m)·Xᵀ(p − y) has the same form as linear regression's.
An SVM maximizes the margin. The hinge loss ignores points with margin ≥ 1, so the boundary depends only on the support vectors.
An RBF kernel exp(−γ‖a − b‖²) gives a non-linear boundary. Its Gram matrix is symmetric, PSD and has ones on the diagonal.

steps.label: Score
steps.detail: z = X @ w + b, one number per example, as in linear regression.

steps.label: Read the score
steps.detail: Logistic: p = σ(z). SVM: the sign of z, with margin y·z.

steps.label: Charge mistakes
steps.detail: Cross-entropy log(1 + e^z) − y·z, or hinge max(0, 1 − y·z), plus an L2 penalty on w.

steps.label: Descend
steps.detail: Gradient (1/m)·Xᵀ(p − y) for logistic; the subgradient over active margins (< 1) for the SVM.

steps.label: Go non-linear
steps.detail: Replace dot products with a kernel such as RBF to bend the boundary.

terms.definition: σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)), mapping a real-valued score to a probability in (0, 1).
The negative log-likelihood of 0/1 labels under predicted probabilities p: −[y·log p + (1 − y)·log(1 − p)].
y·(x·w + b) for labels in {−1, +1}: positive when correct, and larger the further the point is from the boundary.
max(0, 1 − y·z): zero for points beyond the margin, growing linearly for points inside it or misclassified.
The training points on or inside the margin. They alone determine the SVM's decision boundary.
Replacing inner products with a kernel K(a, b) to learn linear boundaries in an implicit, richer feature space.
